beats.lead: The fire destroyed the city. The city's own monument insists it barely touched a life.
beats.text: The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 and burned for four days, destroying roughly 80% of the walled city.
beats.note: It took four of the City's seven gates along with St Paul's Cathedral.

beats.context: burned down in four days. The official death toll was six.

beats.text: The Monument to the fire still carries the line: "Merciless to the wealth and estates of the citizens, it was harmless to their lives."
beats.note: The six recorded dead include a maid who could not escape the bakery where the fire started, and three bodies found mummified by heat inside St Paul's Cathedral.

beats.text: Historians disagree on whether six is real. Adrian Tinniswood puts the toll in single figures; Neil Hanson argues it was several hundred, or quite possibly several thousand.
beats.note: Hanson's case rests on melted glass and iron found in the ruins: evidence the fire burned hotter than a modern crematorium, hot enough to leave no remains at all.

beats.text: One death the toll does include is Robert Hubert, a French watchmaker who confessed to starting the fire and was hanged for it at Tyburn.
beats.note: He had changed his story once already, claiming Westminster before learning the fire never reached there, and a ship's captain later testified Hubert did not land in England until two days after it started.

beats.line: 13,200 houses burned. The monument says six people died. Historians aren't convinced.
